utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration you made yesterday still applies. And Mr. Tolimir is now commencing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. May God speed us on our way today and may God bless us. I bid you all welcome back to the courtroom and may we have a successful day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since we speak the same language I'll ask you a question and please try to make a pause so we don't overlap in order to allow the interpretation to proceed, and I'll try to do the same. Thank you. My first question is from page 1 of the interview that you gave to this Tribunal in Banja Luka on the 27th of June 2009, if you remember. This is D336. Could we please have that displayed in our e-court system. 1D336. Thank you, Aleksandar. 1D336. So that everyone can see what I'm basing my questions on. We can't see that yet. All right, we have it in the English and it's about to come up in our language too, the Serbian. Please look at lines 19 through 21. What is discussed there is the status of a witness. You handed over to the Prosecutor a summons which states that you are a suspect. My question is: Were you under any sort of mental duress when you received a summons as a suspect since you know as a fact that you did not commit any crimes for which you might be prosecuted by this international tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was under no pressure at all. We've clarified that already. I asked them when I came there, they said it was a mistake. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know you tried to clarify that point during the interview but what about since?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no reason to feel any sort of pressure at all because my conscience is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we please go to page 3 of the interview, line 26. Page 3, line 26. In the English, it should be page 4. At line 26, you say, "I was a general administrator." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that position, did you have an overview over the mail being exchanged by the brigade or the codes being used and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would most often be the case, but it was by no means a rule as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps we didn't understand each other properly. I was asking whether an administrator like that would have an insight into the mail being exchanged between the brigade and the battalion, codes and such.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that all the members of the brigade had an insight into all the mail that was coming from the brigade to the battalion, and that included me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about any written documents that were mailed to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sort of thing would normally be opened by the commander, not us. Nevertheless, whatever came by phone we would normally get to look at it. As a rule, there were no special secrets that were kept from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Vanderpuye gets the floor I would like to remind both speakers to slow down and not to overlap. You are starting with your answers immediately after you have heard the question of Mr. Tolimir, but the interpreters must catch everything what you are saying and what Mr. Tolimir is saying. Please pause a little bit between question and answer. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours and everyone. I think there is a -- maybe we can have the witness clarify this. At page 3, line 8, his answer to General Tolimir's question was that, "All members of the brigade had an insight into all of the mail that was coming from the brigade to the battalion, and that included me." I just wanted to make sure that his reference to the insight that was had by brigade members is what he intended to say, as opposed to battalion members. So maybe we can have that clarified for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you have heard what the Prosecutor has said. Could you clarify your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the battalion. Perhaps I misspoke and said brigade. The members of the battalion command saw all the telegrams that were being received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. For the record, my question was: A general administrator, such as the witness, would a person in that position normally look at all the mail being exchanged between the brigade and the battalion? General administrator. That was my question. A person in his position and not any members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E-court, please, page 5 of your statement, sir. Can you please look at line 20, page 5. Page 7 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say at line 20: "In July 1995, the line shifted and there were some movements in July, movements of our battalion because there was this column of people coming from Srebrenica, so engagement of the battalion was 100 per cent." That's lines 21 and 22 of your statement. Based on what you said there, my question: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what sort of movement was at stake. How was the line moved? And what about stepping up engagement up to 100 per cent, what was behind that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some of the people were operating on the ground and that those other men came out and were to protect that area. As far as we were concerned. I don't know what areas this was in relation to. I know that the presence along the line of those mobilised in the battalion was 100 per cent, and that's about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said, "I don't know which area they were going to, and so on and so forth." Please, for the record, when you say I don't know which line they were off to, who, where, who was going through these defence lines and why was combat readiness stepped up? Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber a little bit, because they weren't there, they were not there in the middle of the war, like you and me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This column leaving Srebrenica and then they were securing all these settled areas so they could pass through them, they were protecting certain areas towards the rear of the area, all the villages that were there, and that was about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much but I do have to apologise yet again. Thank you very much, Mr. Interpreter. Again, I have to ask you those leaving Srebrenica were securing these villages. We have to try to distinguish here who was doing the securing and who was leaving Srebrenica. We need to draw some sort of distinction there. Who was leaving Srebrenica, can you tell us that? Which unit did those men belong to and who was securing the villages and settlements along the way? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you because you started too early. It is very difficult for the interpreters today. You are both very fast and you should slow down and pause between both speakers. Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The villages and the rear area, that was the VRS and the rest the army and the people from Srebrenica, the people who lived in Srebrenica, and the VRS were securing our villages that were in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said they were leaving Srebrenica. Did they come under attack or were they attacking the villages that you, the men of the Zvornik Brigade, were defending? Thank you very much. Please can you wait up a little bit before you provide your answer. Thank you very much. Look at the screen before you, look at the transcript, and once it's done, once it stops rolling, you can start answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there to know myself who was attacking whom. There was firing on both sides, but I wasn't there myself to be able to tell you what exactly went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't know if you have the transcript in front of you. As soon as the transcript stops, please start answering your question, but wait for the transcript, for the letters, to stop. Again I have to ask you the same question because of the record. Why did your brigade step up its combat readiness, and what about the people -- you called them people -- were they free to leave Srebrenica or were there some special circumstances there under which these people were leaving as well as their army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all know there was fighting inside Srebrenica and they had to get out somehow. How were they getting out? Of course, there was firing along the way on their way out. It wasn't a peaceful situation, there was firing all over, but again I'm telling you I wasn't there myself, therefore I'm unable to judge the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That wasn't my question, really, was it? You said people were leaving. Can you please explain to the Chamber how exactly people were leaving. And now you've answered. It wasn't some sort of free passage or free movement by the civilians and the people leaving. It was a column trying to get through across your territory, and did that column include both civilians and soldiers? And when I say "soldiers" I mean armed Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our area of responsibility. Not in the area covered by my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about the area of responsibility of your brigade? Were these Muslim armed forces trying to achieve a breakthrough along with the civilian population coming along across the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will have seen that now the question has stopped, but your answer was long time ago. This is not possible to catch that by the interpreters, and for the sake of the record it is necessary to pause. Please wait -- I appreciate that you want to tell everything you know, but please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, sir, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this was all about and what was it that was passing through the area of responsibility of your brigade, and why did your commanders order you to step up your combat readiness up to the 100 per cent level?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the consequences of the attacks coming from the other side and that's probably why the order came to mobilise 100 per cent. You're asking me some questions. I can't answer all these questions, I wasn't a commander myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand why you're answering the way you are, but when you say "the other side" what that means to the Trial Chamber, "the other side," maybe you're talking about the cardinal points as long as you're not specific. Who was this other side?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim army. That's what I mean when I said "the other side."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, what about the members of your battalion? Did they have any contact whatsoever with the Muslim column trying to achieve a breakthrough across the territory that was also the area of responsibility of your brigade? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My battalion had no contact. As for the brigade, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will move on, given the nature of your answers. I never asked you anything about the brigade, did I? Can you please go to page 6 of your statement, line 27. Page 6, line 27, thank you. This is page 9 in the English. Thank you. Thank you very much. I'll read this, if you can see it. Lines 27 and 28. You say there existed a telephone link and some couriers were bringing orders. My question to you, based on what we can see here: Did you receive most of your orders by phone? Was it an uncoded conversation or was it an encrypted conversation? Was this a protected line or not? Thank you very much. And please wait for the transcript to stop.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders would come by the induction telephone line most often. Rarely they arrived as coded messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are talking about telephone connections and induction telephone lines, could you please explain, were those wire lines? So that the Trial Chamber knows what you're talking about. Did you have a wire telephone line with the brigade command where your orders came from or did you have a radio connection with them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a wire connection. We also had a radio communication line, but we used it only very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, when you say coded messages, because you used the word "coded," would you say that codes were only used in teletyped messages or are codes any figures and symbols used in any communication? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the very rare coded telegrams, save for the one that arrived in 1995, I don't know anything about codes. I know that signalsmen or, rather, a signalsman came to decode that message. I was not able to do it; I don't know anything about code system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that the telegram was coded by signalsmen. Were they members of your battalion, of your brigade, or were they borrowed from somewhere else to decode the telegram? Thank you. Please wait for the transcript to stop.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from our battalion. Nobody else arrived from anywhere else. Our own men came to decode the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that they knew how to decipher the code, that they had that from before? Thank you. Please wait for the transcript before you start giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what the system was, what system was in place for decoding messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did it take the signalsman to decode the message? Do you know that? Are you aware of that fact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at lines 7 and 14 on page 7 in the Serbian version, which is page 10 in the English version. Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you about your combat readiness. That's in line 7. And then in line 14, you said, "Yes, we were prepared for a possible attack from the other side. What do I know?" So what did you mean when you say, "The other side"? And what did you mean when you said, "What do I know?" We can't leave the Trial Chamber in the dark about anything that you said. Please wait for the transcript to stop before giving your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose we were expecting an attack from the Muslim side. I suppose that our commanders knew what they were doing. Please do not ask me questions that only a brigade commander can answer. I suppose that they were expecting an attack to come from the Muslim side and that's why they stepped up our combat readiness to full readiness, to 100 per cent combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please do not be angry. I'm not asking you any personal questions. Whatever I ask you are things that need to be clarified for the transcript. I'm not trying to trick you and ask you questions that you're not in a position to answer. And I apologise if you misunderstood my intentions. Could we please display page 8 in your statement, which is page 12 in English. Lines 22 and 32. Please look at the lines in question, line 22 and line 32. In order to avoid reading the entire statement, I have only chosen some characteristic lines on which I'm going to base my questions. You say in line 22, "I believe that that was in the afternoon and I know that he came back in the evening and told us all that." And then in line 32, you say, "That was the gym of the elementary school." Please, can you tell us for the record, who was it who came? Because your subject in the sentence is missing. And then you said, "He told us." You did already say something about that in the cross-examination, but could you now tell us what that person said, who was there to listen to him, and was the entire battalion command there to listen to that story? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our commander, Srecko Acimovic, and he addressed the entire command staff in the evening when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. During the examination-in-chief yesterday, the Prosecutor showed you some photos, and he showed you photo number 2 on page 121. As he explained, that was the second photo of the gym of the elementary school that you had attended, and you said that you had never entered the small building next to the gym and that that small building was probably used as a changing room, as lockers for the kids who attended the school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: At the relevant time, were you in the gym about which Mr. Vanderpuye asked you yesterday? Thank you. Please wait for the transcript to stop.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here you -- on page 10 in the Serbian version of your statement, which is page 14 in English, in line 30, you resumed this statement, and the Prosecutor told you, and this is on page 15 in English, I apologise to everybody -- thank you, Aleksandar, for correcting me -- and while we are waiting for that, I believe you all see it now, the Prosecutor says, "We continue our interview with Mr. Lazarevic and during the break we spent --" thank you -- "during the break -- we spent a few minutes during the break just discussing general issues with the witness and we told him why he had been invited to come here today, and also we invited questions from him." And then we move on to the following page, which is 16 in English -- thank you, Aleksandar -- and the investigator says here, "The witness was wondering why there was the low level people and not the high level people that we were interested in." There was no discussion about his particular evidence. Thank you. In view of this, I would like to know the following: You had several other breaks, did you not? Did you use those breaks to discuss your concerns and issues that were of some interest to you? Did the investigators encourage you to raise those concerns during the breaks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nothing. That was right at the end, when I said to this gentleman, the investigator, that there was no justice. First of all we were mobilised to go to war, and now you are investigating me here, you're interviewing me here, so there is no justice in this world. That's what I said to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. Yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, you answered several questions put to you by Mr. Vanderpuye and you told us that your commander disobeyed the order and wouldn't assign any of your men to execute men who were detained in the elementary school of the village where he resided. Now my question: Did anybody from your battalion command have to face charges for disobeying an order which was contrary to rules and prevalent laws? Thank you. Please wait for the transcript to stop.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was ever in a position to face charges because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer the following question: Since you have mostly related things that you heard from others, since you personally did not participate in any of the events, my question is this: Is your evidence second-hand evidence and do you know -- well, first answer that, and please wait for the transcript to stop before giving your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I heard from my commander, but I believe that the essence of my evidence are the telegrams that arrived in the brigade when I was there. This is what I am here for, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Did you personally see the telegram that you are testifying about? Thank you. And do you know who recorded the telegram in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know who had received the telegram. It may have been me. But we were all present while the lads were decoding it, and everybody was wondering about its content. So everybody knew about the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell me and the Trial Chamber: Do you know whether your commander, battalion commander, testified? And if not, do you know if he's ever going to come here to testify about the same events you are testifying about? If you don't know, you can just simply say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was here once. I don't know whether he will be called to testify again. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for the answers that you have provided. Thank you about the information provided about your commander. I hope that he will come to testify in these proceedings so we will have questions for you [as interpreted]. Thank you very much for coming here today to clarify things that I was not clear about, neither me nor the OTP nor the Trial Chamber. God bless.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was my cross-examination. I would like to thank you, thank everybody who have been following, and I apologise on my part and on the part of the witness because the two of us have been speaking very fast. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was indeed a very hard morning for the interpreters and the Court Recorder. Thank you for the assistance. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I'm sure you'll be relieved to know what I don't. I would point out, though, in respect of General Tolimir's question that the commander of the 2nd Battalion is on our witness list. He's a 92 bis with cross witness and we do expect to have him available for the Trial Chamber to hear evidence from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination in this trial. Thank you very much for your attendance here and that you came to The Hague again. Now you are free to return to your normal activities and to travel home. Thank you very much again. The Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can you tell us, is the next witness ready for testifying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He is, Mr. President. I know that my colleague Mr. Thayer has been following the proceedings, and so I expect him down momentarily, and I believe the witness is already in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session for just a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take the opportunity -- I take the opportunity to indicate that at the moment, the Chamber is planning -- perhaps this is important for Mr. McCloskey, if he could listen to what I'm talking about. At the moment, the Chamber is planning to sit on Friday afternoon instead of the cancelled hearing on Wednesday because of the plenary of the Judges. That means, if we have such progress as yesterday and today, I would like to ask the Prosecution if the next witness for Monday would be available if we are finishing the current witness, which is the upcoming witness, earlier. Perhaps you can give an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. That witness, I'm informed, has -- is not scheduled to come here in time to be able to testify for Friday afternoon. That -- and based on the estimates of this particular witness, it looks like we would be going into Friday, though, as you may be correct, we may end up finishing early, but given who this witness is, he's a brigade commander, we think it's going to go into Friday. Perhaps -- as we do, Mr. Gajic and I did speak about the length of time last night, for Colonel Trivic, and Mr. Gajic could perhaps -- perhaps he has more information. He thought it was going to be over the three hours he estimated, that's why we thought it would go in, especially looking at today, but today was a little shorter than we thought, so perhaps Mr. Gajic can help us with that estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original scheduling was that the witness Trivic should testify two days. If you start with him now, if we are sitting on Friday, nearly three days of testimony available, and therefore you should consider the possibility to call another witness for Friday to save court time. That was the intention of my questioning. Mr. Gajic, could you say anything in relation to that witness? Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the OTP wants to wrap up within this week with Mr. Trivic, we will not be opposing that. Of course, as long as their examination-in-chief is not too long. We should have sufficient time to finish him on Friday if they take up the whole of today and tomorrow, or, rather, the Thursday. The main thing is to keep him available over the weekend so that Mr. McCloskey does not need to call another witness. It really depends on the time the OTP takes with their examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are aware of this potential gap. Mr. Thayer has been aware of it, as have I, and we have been working with Ms. Gallagher to see if she may be able to help fill it by an exhibit that I have talked briefly about with Mr. Gajic. I haven't talked to him recently about it but of course I will as it looks like if that is going to be an opening. Mr. Thayer is fully aware of it, as am I, that this may be appearing, this opening, and we are doing our best to fill it, and we understand the Court's concern and agree with it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I raised this matter only because we have -- we are really quite fast in this -- at the beginning of this week. Now we should call the next witness. He should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify something. I just wanted to clarify that I misspoke with respect to the two witnesses that I spoke about on page 16 of today's transcript. They are not live witnesses, they are both 92 bis witnesses, so their evidence is before the Trial Chamber already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are, and I wish you a successful working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Do you receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The ear-phones should be moved a bit. I am afraid that you will lose them. That seems to be much better. Would you please read aloud the affirmation, the solemn declaration on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First the Prosecutor will examine you, and later on, the accused, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours, good morning to the Defence, good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My name is Mirko Trivic, born 1949 in Gradiska municipality, which used to be called Bosanska Gradiska at the time and was part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying in this courtroom over a period of four days in May of 2007?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And since you arrived on Sunday, have you had an opportunity to listen to your testimony, or parts of it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Most of it. Most of my testimony. I listened to it again. I think there remains a third, and that was on my last courtroom day. There was a lot of material to deal with, it's as simple as that, and perhaps it would have required a little more time to listen to the entire thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we are moving a little bit more quickly than we had anticipated, so unfortunately, you haven't had an opportunity to review or listen to your entire testimony. Can you first attest that what you have listened to, the first three days, if I understand you correctly, accurately reflects what you said during your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those are the materials and those are the statements that I made. There is nothing contentious about it, from my perspective, in terms of the way I reflected on those issues and the assertions that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on the three days of your testimony which you've listened to so far, do you have any reason to believe that the remaining testimony that you haven't had a chance to listen to again doesn't accurately reflect what your testimony was in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I don't think one should expect that I would change anything. I finished listening to the material as far as the portion that concerned the war zones was concerned. I think that is the last part of day 3, so that wasn't completed either, then. I don't think there was anything that might be misleading. I don't think there is anything that might lead me to a different conclusion or a different opinion on all those theoretical issues, which is what I choose to call them, regarding the rules and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And based on what you've listened to thus far, I take it there were no misinterpretations or technical errors that you noticed in the audio of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: None that I noticed. It's not that I went back to anything specific. I'm sure you have the transcript yourself and there were some corrections being made as we went along during my testimony. There may have been some misinterpretations there on the spot that were corrected, but regarding your questions or the questions of the Defence team, some corrections were being made in our stride, as it were, and that's all I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've pretty much answered my next question, but just so it's clear on the record, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked during those four days in 2007, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I have to be precise with my answer. I'll try not to oversimplify. My opinions have not changed in terms of the way the facts were interpreted at the time or the facts themselves. Now, would I answer the very same question in the very same way? That is open to debate. One would have to analyse the substance of an answer before one could provide a response to that. I do, however, assume that my responses at the time would cover over 95 per cent of the same questions today. I would tend to agree with at least 95 of those answers, but it's been some time and it's very difficult for me to ascertain that my answers would be verbatim what they were those -- all those years ago. I hope you understand the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that's clear for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P1196 and 1197, the witness's testimony in the Popovic trial, the former exhibit being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour for the record, I'd like to indicate that P1196 shall be admitted as Exhibit P1443, under seal, and P1197 shall be admitted as Exhibit P1444, under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have a problem to understand. Have these documents been preliminarily MFI'd at a former stage of these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic? I see you want to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Good morning to all. Mr. President, I'm looking at our e-court and I see that the numbers have been MFI'd. Mr. Thayer also gave us the corresponding P number and not the corresponding 65 ter number. I think that might lead to some confusion, if we were to renumerate, to assign new numbers to these exhibits. One thing that I find particularly confusing, and perhaps someone can clear that up for me: Why are the smaller numbers being transformed into bigger numbers? Because there might be a void that would require filling at a later stage. I fail to understand the situation, I'm afraid. It might be a good idea to keep the numbers that have been used for the MFI'ing of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that would be the position of the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was under the impression that for the witnesses for whom we have gone through the labourious process among all the parties of submitting the exhibit list and having the P numbers assigned, we would retain those until those witnesses are exhausted. So P1196 is formerly 65 ter number 6738. P1197 is formerly 65 ter number 6739. And indeed, they have been both been MFI'd, according to our prior procedure, that I think we are escaping shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem was that I didn't have this list of MFI numbers in front of me, and indeed both exhibits should be received and will be received with the numbers 1197 and 1196, and I think the first one is under seal -- the second one is under seal. 1196. Mr. Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, I would like to indicate that the previous numbers given to P1196 and 1197, which is P1443 and 1444, is hereby withdrawn and P1196 is admitted under seal while P1197 is also admitted under the same number. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think now we have it clear on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would also tender -- Mr. President, maybe I could benefit from a little bit of guidance from the Court. Does Your Honour have the Registrar's internal memorandum for the old regime? Because I'll be working with that list, hopefully that will assist the Trial Chamber in seeing what our exhibits precisely are, and if I can hand my copy up to the court officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. We hope to clarify the situation. Now I have it in front of me and I think we can proceed as usual. As you will have realised, on a request by the Registry, we changed the system a bit and hopefully -- hopefully with -- to the benefit of both parties and the Chamber and especially the Registry, to avoid complications. Before you are tendering these documents, Mr. Thayer, could you indicate if they are all on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think they all are with the exception of two, Mr. President. Actually, sorry, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your previous list, you added a star to the 65 ter number 06745 and 65 ter 06747. Usually -- and to three others at the end, two others at the end of the list. That was normally an indication that they were not included into the 65 ter exhibit list but now I was told that 65 ter 06740 and 06746 are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President. What the asterisk typically denoted were exhibits which were part of the original 92 bis package. And during this whole process of numbering, we found additional exhibits that needed to be put on the exhibit list for the witness, and that's what the asterisk is. As to your first question, which documents were not on the 65 ter list, basically the documents that are the 6700 series on this list were not on the 65 ter list. These are documents that were primarily Defence exhibits that were shown to the witness during his cross-examination. So they were made part of the 92 bis package, as I think everyone is aware, but typically they would not be added wholesale to the 65 ter list because they were part of the 92 bis package, so frequently those exhibits we waited until the decision of the Trial Chamber before assigning them 65 ter numbers. So we can see that there are a number of exhibits here beginning with, if we just look at the list, 6740, 6741, -2, -3, -4, -5, -6, -7, 6749, 6750, and I think that is the total of the exhibits which weren't on the 65 ter list, so per our usual procedure we would move orally to add them to the 65 ter list given their integral part of the prior record being primarily Defence exhibits shown to the witness during his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, is there any concern on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just checked the documents we are talking about and I have no concerns to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, they will be added to the 65 ter exhibit list. And I'm referring to those Mr. Thayer has mentioned on page 25 of today's transcript. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, working with the P numbers that are on the list, if I could, that will save a little bit of time. I don't know if the Registrar needs me to read out the actual 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't do that, to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you, Mr. President. Then the Prosecution would tender P1198 to P1208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are all documents used with this witness in the -- and admitted in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received with these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will withdraw its tender of P01209, which is 65 ter 6745. That is, frankly, mooted by the witness's presence now. This was a stipulation that was entered into between one of the accused's Defence teams in the Popovic trial. After the close of evidence, there was a technical issue concerning a document that I will be spending some time with Colonel Trivic on, and rather than opening up both the Defence and the Prosecution cases in that case, we simply arrived at a stipulation which I think will, frankly, be mooted by the witness's testimony, so we would withdraw that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Thayer beat me to the punch. I was about to raise the issue myself. As far as the exhibit that has been MFI'd P1208 [as interpreted], this was stipulated in a previous case between the OTP and the Defence. P1209. Could that be stricken from the record, then, please. May I just put forward the position of our Defence? We shall always be raising objections whenever a document is being tendered into evidence from a previous case, a previous trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understood you correctly, Mr. Gajic. Please help me. You have mentioned P1208. Did you misspeak or what is -- what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, P1209. I'm not sure if I misspoke or it was misrecorded. Mr. Tolimir claims that I said 1209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we have it clear on the record. I take it that you don't object that the Prosecution is withdrawing this document from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree that that should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would additionally tender P1210 to P1223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received with these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we will also move to withdraw P1224, which is 65 ter 6747, the document that was not included in the 92 bis package. It was only a very brief portion, as it turns out, was read to the witness, and I don't think, given the Trial Chamber's practice of requiring us to use the document somehow with the witness, I'd rather just save some court time and withdraw that exhibit. The pertinent part, as I said, is in the record, it was read to the witness, and I don't think we need to go through any motions to admit the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no need to decide about that at the moment. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I remember correctly, and I don't have a specific reference at hand, the document that Mr. Thayer is addressing was used in the Popovic case with a witness. I believe that deserves to be admitted. This is P1224, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was admitted in the Popovic case through another witness, not with the current witness. There is no need to discuss this at the moment. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P1225 to 1226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was expecting this problem. Mr. Thayer, pursuant to our Rules and the procedure in this trial, we should see if you are dealing with that with this witness. Because it was not used with this -- and admitted, especially not admitted, through this witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I confused this category with the other categories. You can see we have a number of primarily Defence exhibits which were shown to this witness in the Popovic trial but which were admitted through other witnesses. They are, as I said, primarily Defence witness -- Defence exhibits. I do think, for the sake of Your Honours' ability to fully have the record before you, and the documents, they should be admitted. Again, he was shown each of those documents, questioned on them by Defence counsel, and in some cases by the Prosecution. In this case, I would ask the Trial Chamber to permit the admission of these documents without having to use each one of them with the witness. Or, in the alternative, to maintain them in MFI status so that the Trial Chamber can refer to them at its leisure in the future. But it will entail a substantial repetition of the witness's prior testimony to have to use these documents individually in order to have them admitted under the current procedure. In the alternative, I suppose I could just pop them up on e-court and ask him if he remembers seeing it in the Popovic case, and if that suffices for the Trial Chamber, that will expedite matters somewhat as opposed to engaging in a substantive discussion with him about each document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, your position is clear. We will come back to that later. We have time enough with this witness to make a finding. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would similarly tender in this category, given -- recognising our colloquy, 1227A through D, 1228A through C, 1229A and C, and 1230 to 1232, and that constitutes the remainder of the documents in that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The position of the Chamber is the same. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just note a couple of corrections to the transcript and to our exhibit list just so there is no confusion. The first is with respect to P1227C, an intercept used by one of the Defence teams, the time is 6 -- 0658 hours, not 0656 hours. The same goes for the next exhibit, P1227D. It is the same conversation but I think, as the Trial Chamber will recall, occasionally different intercept operators were a minute or two off, and that explains the difference here. Similarly, with respect to P1228B, the time of that intercept is 0755 hours, not 0748 hours. I'd also like to note that in the transcript there was an incorrect exhibit number called out by Defence counsel for General Pandurevic, and this is at transcript page 1196. There is a reference to Exhibit 7D425, and that exhibit is actually 7D550, which is the exhibit listed on our exhibit list. Defence counsel simply mixed up his numbers but it's clearly referring to 7D550, and that, in this case, is P1207. And lastly, we have a -- as an exhibit, P94, the book of photographs from Mr. Ruez. The relevant page number for this Trial Chamber's purposes is page 250. The pagination changed just a little bit between the Popovic version and the version that's before the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, I think I've got enough time to read the 92 ter summary before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In July 1995, the witness was serving as the commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, based in Sokolac. He retired from the VRS with the rank of Colonel in 2002. Prior to the Srebrenica operation in July 1995, he received a preparatory order from the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic, according to which the witness pulled approximately 200 men from his brigade's battalions to form a combat group for the operation. His combat group also included a tank platoon and a mortar platoon. His combat group arrived in the Zeleni Jadar area on 5 July, and the witness reported first to the command of the Bratunac Brigade and then to an observation point near the Drina Corps forward command post as Pribicevac. At this observation point General Krstic issued instructions to the witness and the other brigade commanders regarding the Krivaja 95 operation. In addition, Drina Corps intelligence officer Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, per customary procedure, briefed them about the estimates of the enemy's strength and deployment. The witness testified that the main objective of the Krivaja 95 operation was to separate and narrow the size of the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, in view of the sabotage and terrorist actions from them. The witness said that he was not aware of any plan or operation directed by the VRS to cut off the resupply of DutchBat and to restrict the inflow of humanitarian aid to the Srebrenica enclave. The witness further testified that the VRS forces participating in the Krivaja 95 operation were supposed to avoid conflicts with the UN personnel at their check-points and that the target of the operation was not the UN, the town of Srebrenica itself, or the population. The witness's command post during the Krivaja 95 operation was in the village of Jasenova, where he slept each night during the operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I believe that the interpreter has not interpreted you correctly, and as I'm looking at the transcript, I'm looking at the part where you were talking about the objective of the operation. The witness says, and so on and so forth, that operation 1995 was not targeted at the United Nations but the population of Srebrenica. I believe that's what I heard in the interpretation. So could you please repeat that portion in order for the interpreter to repeat the interpretation of that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll pick up with that sentence, Mr. President. The witness testified that the VRS forces participating in the Krivaja 95 operation were supposed to avoid any conflicts with the UN personnel at their check-points and that the target of the operation was not the UN, the town of Srebrenica itself, or the population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much better. That was actually now correct. The first time round, the interpreter used a wrong word which gave a totally different meaning. At least, that's how I understood it in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any misinterpretation, Mr. Thayer, you are saying in your summary that the target was not the UN, and it was not the town of Srebrenica itself, or the population of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It could be understood in a different way, indeed. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The witness's command post during the Krivaja 95 operation was in the village of Jasenova, where he slept each night during the operation. He described the activities and movement of his forces between 6 and 11 July 1995 as they headed in a northerly direction towards Srebrenica with forces from the Zvornik Brigade's Drina Wolves on his right and forces from the Birac Brigade on his left. He identified himself in video footage of VRS forces as they approached, then entered Srebrenica town. He testified that his unit did not fire upon the town of Srebrenica and that he did not observe, notice, or hear of any other units firing upon the town itself, nor did he observe any artillery damage to the town when he entered it. He further testified that the people who went to the UN base in Potocari did so of their own will, and that when General Mladic offered the Muslim population a choice of whether to stay or leave, they decided to evacuate themselves from Srebrenica. In the morning of 12 July, at the location in Bojna near a TV repeater, he was given the assignment to move toward the Jahorina feature via the village of Vijogor. At Vijogor that afternoon, General Krstic ordered him to report to the Bratunac Brigade command post for a meeting at 2100 hours that evening. He arrived at that meeting on time, having passed through Potocari en route and seeing crowds of people there. About an hour later General Mladic arrived, congratulated them, and gave Krstic the order to prepare for an operation against Zepa. Orders were also given to Drina Corps units, in cooperation with the MUP, to secure the road from Srebrenica towards Vlasenica via Bratunac. The intelligence they had at the time indicated that several thousand members of the 28th Division were attempting to cross through VRS-held territory to reach ABiH-held territory. Also during this meeting, Pandurevic suggested that the troops be rested and replaced, but Mladic overruled him. However, Mladic agreed to address the troops the next morning, 13 July, before they moved to Zepa. Mr. President, I see we are slightly over the time for the break. I have three more paragraphs to read and I can interrupt the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should conclude that and we have the break a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The witness testified that he does not recall any mention during this meeting of what the procedure would be if any military-aged men were captured or surrendered to VRS forces. He stated that he was not aware, at the time of this meeting, that Muslim men had been separated from their families that day in Potocari, nor did he receive any information that there may have been as many as a thousand military-aged men in Potocari. He further testified that there was no discussion at this meeting about placing captured or surrendered Muslim men in detention locations in and around Bratunac, nor was there any mention of a decision to kill all the men of military age. Following the meeting, the officers present were served an organised dinner in the Bratunac Brigade command building. In the morning of 13 July, Generals Mladic and Krstic addressed the witness's troops to motivate them for the impending Zepa operation, after which Krstic ordered the witness and his forces to be in the village of Krivace in Zepa by 1900 hours that day. The witness again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down a bit, I think, for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. The witness again travelled through Potocari en route to Zepa and observed people being loaded onto vehicles. He passed by the football field in Nova Kasaba which was filled with prisoners seated on the ground and guarded by MPs from the Main Staff's 65th Protection Regiment. When the witness arrived in the Krivace area, he communicated his arrival to the Drina Corps forward command post located at an elevation called Solila. The witness then described his participation in the Zepa operation, including the movements of his forces and the forward command post from Solila to Godjenje village. He also described a cease-fire on 19 July and a lunch the next day in honour of General Zivanovic's retirement and General Krstic's promotion in his place as commander of the Drina Corps. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the first break now. We will resume five minutes past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, our apologies for the delay. All judges were occupied by another commitment during the break which took more time than expected. Secondly, the Chamber would like to confirm that we will sit on Friday in the afternoon, instead of Wednesday, that means tomorrow, this week, because of a plenary of the Judges. Thirdly, the motion, Mr. Thayer, to admit those documents which were not used -- not admitted through this witness in the previous case, in the Popovic case, is -- will not be accepted. We will deny it, because you know since 21st -- 24th of February this year the course the Chamber will take, that for those documents not admitted through the witness, it is necessary to show that they are an indispensable part of the testimony in the prior case, and there must be a certain showing to be able to accept that. There is no need to go into details because we have dealt with that several times, and the Chamber is in a certain way surprised that this problem arises now again. Mr. Thayer, please carry on with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I noted that while I was finishing up your summary, you were taking some notes and I just wanted to make sure that you didn't hear anything that you thought was incorrect or that needed clarification. So before I go on to my next series of questions, I just wanted to give you the opportunity, in case there was something. If not, then that's fine. I'll just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I would like to say something. Not because things were incorrect but because of some terms, two or three terms, which are disputable. The first one was that there was no fire opened on Srebrenica, and that's something that I didn't use. When you say fire being open, it can be construed as a game. As a soldier, I conclude that there were no operations targeting Srebrenica. The second term that was used was something that contained the word "artillery destruction" or something to that effect. Maybe it would be better to use there was no destruction in town. There were no destroyed facilities. That's what I said in my statement. And the third term that was used by yourself, I may have used it myself in answering your questions in my previous testimony, concerned the football pitch in Nova Kasaba. You used the term there were "detainees" who were sitting in the football pitch, and I believe that a better term to use, or something that I would use. Was "disarmed enemy troops," because those were not people from Potocari, those who had surrendered. Those were disarmed troops that were on their way to link up with the BiH army. In the meantime, they were prevented from doing that by men who disarmed them and who confined them in an area where they would be confined until further proceedings. That's the remarks I wanted to share with you, and I'd like to say that the rest of what you have read out was pretty much correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. We'll perhaps get to some of those issues in a little while. Let me begin by showing you a couple of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P104, please. And if we could go to page 12 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can tell you, Colonel, in a moment we'll look at a portion of this map a little closer. What I wanted to do was start with this map, which obviously is a slightly larger view. Take a moment, if you would, and see if you can acquaint yourself, reacquaint yourself, with some of these locations as they are marked here and just moving from left to right. I would just draw your attention to where the map indicates the Jela restaurant, the 65th Protection Regiment base, the command post of the VRS's Main Staff, and then moving from north to south, the Krivace forward command post, the Podzeplje forward command post, the Godjenje forward command post, all the way down to the Okresanica check-point and the Borike forward command post and what is referred to as the Borike villa. Please just take a moment and orient yourself. This is a VRS map, no doubt you can identify it as such, perhaps not exactly which map it is, but my first question is: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, number 1, whether you recognise and are familiar with the locations depicted here?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with all the locations depicted here, and they were exactly as you can see them. The Borike villa was a motel, which is why it is called the Borike villa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed, and for the record, this is ERN 0701-3282. Now if we could go to the next page in e-court, please, and we'll look at a slightly enlarged image here. You referred in your testimony to reporting to the Krivace IKM by radio communications as opposed to in person. Do you recall that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that's -- that was upon my arrival. As I arrived at the Krivace sector, together with my unit, or rather, my unit and myself, I reported at the sector where the forward command post had been established. I don't see the Solila feature here and I didn't report there personally. I radioed in that the unit had arrived at the location where it was to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe if we could blow up the portion just around the Krivace IKM and Podzeplje IKM that will help a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see the Solila feature. It is in the village of Krivace. The village obviously comprises a larger area than the Solila feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, can you confirm that the word "Solila" is in fact inside this little purple circle where the Krivace IKM has been identified? Can you see the word "Solila"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber what the IKM there actually consisted in when you had occasion to personally report there? Was it a pre-existing building? Was it a command post that had been used previously, or just tents or -- just give the Trial Chamber an idea.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I have just said, and I said it before, in answering either your questions or questions from the Defence, I arrived in the village of Krivace and I visited the IKM at the Solila sector two days later or maybe even three days later. On the day when I arrived at the sector where my unit was deployed, I radioed in at the command post that the unit had arrived. When I visited the forward command post, I noticed that elements had been developed which are normally developed for the corps command in order to enable the functioning of the unit. There were tents for the commander, for the ops room; in other words, everything that was conducive to the command function of the units and -- was there. So there were no pre-existing buildings or any fixed features, there were just tents and everything that went with the tents in terms of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just told us that you radioed in, basically, when you arrived in the Krivace area. Can describe what types of communications facilities were located at this Krivace IKM. You described all the necessary elements of a forward command post. What kind of communication facilities were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of communication facilities is something that a communications officer could tell you about. However, I can confirm that there were things there such as the mobile communication centre on a vehicle. The chief of communications in the corps command was the one who established the communication system by moving from one place to another the mobile communications centre. There was a relay in Veliki Zep nearby and through that he linked up the entire system to make it possible to communicate with all the IKMs in the area. There was nothing else, just that vehicle that had arrived and that made it possible to establish the entire system, to put the entire communications system in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just on that topic, sir, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what types of communication equipment you are talking about when you describe this mobile communications vehicle. What type of actual communications equipment, mechanisms, are we talking about? If you can just put it in simple terms for us, as simple as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to put it in very simple terms. The equipment that the vehicle had was very specific equipment that is necessary and that is linked to certain relays. There was Veliki Zep and there was also Zlovrh, a feature where I was injured. That was a facility that belonged to the former JNA which was built as part of the system of the former state and it was used for All People's Defence, for communications across Yugoslavia. And there was another facility in Han Pijesak, there was one in Veliki Zep, or rather, in Zlovrh. Now, let's go back to that vehicle. That vehicle also had teletype equipment for coded messages and, to put things even in more simple terms, that was predecessor of pagers or the current mobile telephone system. For subordinated brigades, there were other types of communications, for example, wire connections, which were used to protect data, to intercept other communications. But it was not the signals officer in the corps command who made those decisions, it was the subordinated units who made those decisions. And if it is planned for the units to be deployed for a longer time, then wire communications are established with the command for a more simpler communication. The units, the brigade commands and the corps command, had systems of protection. We could establish protected communication through the mobile communication system because there were radio sets in the subordinated command and in that vehicle, so we could talk freely without disclosing the contents of that conversation for anybody who may have been listening in. And could you please not ask me any more about the communications profession, because this is the extent of my knowledge about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that certainly your experience as a professional officer has enabled you to give us a pretty good idea of what the guts of the communications capabilities were when you were in Zepa. Let me just ask you a couple of other follow-up questions. This mobile communications vehicle, I take it from what you've told us, was dealing with radio communications as opposed to you just referred to wire communications. Is that correct? And if so, can you just explain to me a little bit about what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That vehicle, when the command post is developed further -- the objective of every system of communications or the centre of communications, is to use open communication as little as possible, in order to prevent interception and the disclosing information to the enemy. The vehicle that we had also had the telephone capabilities to all the units and within the command, with the Vlasenica command post and the staff. This was a very specific vehicle which also provided for the development of telephone lines, wire lines. The difference between certain systems of communication lies in the fact that wire communication or telephone combination -- communication is connected to a small switchboard that every command has, and from there lines, wire lines, are extended to our main switchboard in the brigade commands. So the different lines indicate that coded messages are sent via teleprinter messages, radio communications that we used, those of us who were not signalsmen, we talked to each other verbally, whereas coded messages were printed. Radio communications enabled us to protect the voice or the contents of the conversation so the recipient would receive the message but not -- nothing was on air for anybody who may have been listening in. There were special types of equipment that would be connected to both ends. And wire communication lines was what they were. I don't think that I have to go into details of those. I don't know if I've answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You have, Colonel. Just one other question: The Trial Chamber has heard occasional references to, for example, an induction phone. Can you explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the telephone that I described. All units had them. And when you developed wire connections, the end user could call the switchboard. He would turn a handle, he would create induction, and then the telephone would be -- would ring at the switchboard that you wanted to call, and the switchboard operator would pick up and the person who made the call then says who they want to be put through. So it's like any other switchboard, a very classical switchboard. I believe that you're familiar with the situation. For example, you call a hotel reception, and then you say, Can you put me through to a certain room. Now things have gone -- have been modernised, but in the army we had switchboards which were connected to, for example, ten different induction telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, does that induction phone require a wire connection or is that ultimately a radio wave communication at some point?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a wire connection. It was a wire connection. I don't know whether you heard me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Thank you. Now, let's just move down this map a little bit. We can just keep it where it is. Thank you. We can just keep it where it was, I'm sorry. We can just go back, thanks. Moving, drawing your attention to the Podzeplje IKM, can you tell the Trial Chamber what that was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Krivace was the IKM of the Drina Corps, and Podzeplje I believe was my own IKM. At the moment when I took over the role from the Zvornik Brigade and engaged in active combat, it was necessary for my reserves to be deployed for combat, for engagement, and I had to rearrange my command post in order to be able to monitor the deployment and combat activities of my units. The Podzeplje IKM did not function as an IKM of the Drina Corps. And I'm taken by surprise at the moment. So far, I've not seen in any of the documents this feature called Podzeplje IKM. I believe it was my own command post when it was moved from Jasenova to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can certainly look at a document that you were shown in the Popovic trial, which refers to, I think as you've just --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: One more thing, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just finish my question, then I'll let you answer. We can certainly show you a document where this IKM is specifically referred to, I think, as you've noted, as your IKM. So if you like, I can show that document to you. It was shown to you in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I would like to see that, to jog my memory. It could have been part of the command of another unit. Yes, I would like it to jog my memory. I don't want to arrive at erroneous conclusions or erroneous assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, while we're pulling that document out, can you tell us what facilities, if any, were present at this location, this Podzeplje IKM, when you arrived there? Had it been used previously, for example, by any other unit as some kind of command post? Was there a fixed structure there or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I believe that one part of the command of a unit from the 65th Protection Regiment was there, and I believe that my command arrived in that sector, as far as I can remember. My memory would have to be refreshed and I would like to see the document that I may have seen before. I would like to see it described. I believe that something was already there, that some communications facilities already existed in the area, that something had already been developed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, and just to clarify, that something that may have already been there, are you referring to the presence of 65th Protection Regiment elements being there previously, or were you telling us that this 65th Protection Regiment presence at this Podzeplje IKM was only during the Zepa operation when you were there, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I believe that some of their troops were already there and the command elements of an inferior unit were there, and as you can see in the map, there were some troops that protected the area in the direction of [indiscernible] and Krivace. In other words, there were those elements pre-existing, not only at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, let's look at P1225. This is one of the notorious group of documents that I tendered previously, so we are having a chance to use it. Sir, if you would take a moment and refamiliarise yourself with this document. If we could scroll up just a tad so we can catch the -- I'm sorry, the other way, please. Yeah. There we go. We can see the operational name, Stupcanica 95, in the upper right-hand corner, but take a moment, Colonel, when you're ready for the page to be turned, and just for the record, this is 13 July 1995, attack order, emanating from the Drina Corps command, forward command post in Krivace, sent to various commands of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I've read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just note before we turn the page, if we look at the bottom of paragraph 4, it refers to the objective of liberating and clearing the Serbian Podrinje of Muslim forces and eliminating the enclaves with combat readiness at 0800 hours on the 14th of July. And I believe you've testified previously that that was the order that you were given, that there was to be combat readiness for 0800 on the 14th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the very bottom of the page here, we see the heading, "Krivace command post" with tasks. And if we could go to the next page, we can see the various tasks enumerated, 2, 3, and 4. And if we could scroll over to the left, please, in the B/C/S version, just -- I'm sorry, the other way, to the left. Thank you. Do you see right above -- and we need to scroll down in the English version, please. We can see right above item 5, the heading, "Command post in the village of Podzeplje." Number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Point 5 -- point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Right below point 4, above point 5, the heading, "Command post in the village of Podzeplje." And it indicates that the Romanija Motorised Brigade in reserve in the village of Podzeplje area. That's you; is that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I am the Romanija brigade, that's my brigade, but what it says right above, the command post in the Podzeplje area, that is in reference to the Zvornik Brigade. That is the last thing you see in item 4. They are establishing a command post in Podzeplje. But my own unit, as you see in item 5, has not had an assigned post assigned to it yet. The only thing that it said is I'm in the reserve in the Podzeplje area, which automatically means that my command post is in Podzeplje.
