My command post too is in Podzeplje but we don't see that specially pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you should perhaps with the witness try to find out the original B/C/S version, which is where this seems to be, this third paragraph of item 4, and not the headline for item 5. The design of the page is different in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. The command post in the village of Podzeplje is a heading that refers, if you like -- well, we can go back. Let's go back to the prior page, page 1. We can see items 1, 2, 3 and 4, and that portion ends with combat readiness at 0800 hours on the 14th of July 1995. The next heading is Krivace command post. And the task of the units begins at paragraph 5 with subs 1 through 4, if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, who was based at the Krivace command post, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: If I may, in relation to the remark that the Presiding Judge made, I would still like to clarify one thing. Item 4, the command post in Podzeplje village is not in reference to the next item. That's not the title of the next paragraph. That is the end of item 4. It is not that I'm trying to preach here or necessarily explain anything to you, but could we please go back to page 1? There is something else that I wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, please, let me just stop you right there. Let's stick with the task at hand. If we go to page 1 -- let's go back to page 1, please -- let's just try to make this crystal clear. There is a reference to the Krivace command post, and again my question to you is: What does that heading or footer or however you want to refer to it, what does that pertain to, the Krivace command post? Why is that phrase there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. Just to make this perfectly clear, up to item 4, everything that is there, up to item 4 and before item 5 begins, it's all in relation to the corps. Item 1, the assessment of the situation as far as the enemy is concerned. Item 2, the assessment of the situation among one's own ranks and the ranks of the neighbours. 3, corps units; 4, corps commander decision. And then, within that decision, the commander determines readiness and also the corps's command post. Item 5 begins with something in relation to the subordinate units, and each of the items have one final sentence designating the command post of the unit that the paragraph or the item is in relation to. Each paragraph or item ends with a sentence that determines the command post of the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, if we can go to the next page, and let's just do this systematically. This is why I just wanted to take our time and go through each of these elements. If we see number 1, which actually begins on the prior page in B/C/S -- if we can go back just for Colonel Trivic's benefit in the B/C/S to page 1. We see under number 5, there appears to be a number 1, and that indicates the first Milici Light Infantry Brigade and the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade shall attack, and then it gives an axis and then it gives a task. And if we go to the next page in B/C/S, we see a number 2, a similar provision for the Vlasenica Brigade; a task and an axis. Number 3, the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, an axis and a task. But so far we don't see any command post indicated for any of these units. We get to number 4, we have the Zvornik Brigade and then we have this reference to the command post in the village of Podzeplje. So the question is: First, does that reference to the command post in the village of Podzeplje mean that only the unit in number 4 had its command post there, or all of the units in numbers 1 through 4, or does it mean something else? Because, as we can see from items 1 through 4, there is only one listing of any command post. Each of those individual brigade assignments doesn't have its own command post listed here in this document. So that is my question to you, is: What is this reference, command post in the village of Podzeplje, referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think I understand. Subitem 1 within item 5, the Milic, Vlasenica, Podrinjska, 5th and all the way up to the Zvornik Brigade, there is no reference to the command post there. What is meant is that they used their own command post which, up until this point in time in the combat operations, while holding the lines in the defence areas, they were using the existing command posts. In relation to the Zvornik Brigade, it was necessary to determine a location. Why? Because the Zvornik Brigade used some of its forces to leave its defence area. A component left my area and went to a new area. Of course, my superior command had to determine a new location but not in a formal way. They didn't formally determine a place where I was to establish a command post. It had to be determined in such a way that we could establish an appropriate system of communications so that one could get the command system off the ground, in a manner of speaking. That's why it was necessary to determine for the Zvornik Brigade the area in which it would be establishing its command post. And you see if you look at the next thing, the Romanija brigade, which also arrived from somewhere outside its existing defence area, if I can put it that way, outside its base, no command location was determined in Podzeplje although they were outside their own Defence zone, but suffice it to say that the Romanija brigade was in the reserve in the Podzeplje area. As soon as I knew that, I as a commander and my signals officer knew that they would be setting up a system of communications where they were in the reserve. I'm there, I'm on stand-by, and my units are waiting to be included in the combat disposition, if you get my point, and that is the gist of the discrepancy between these two. Some place you find it and some place you don't. Throws who were outside their zones had to be given a general area to establish their command post. Those who were operating from within their own zones had no need of a new command post being determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So if we go to item 7, then, and if we could go to the next page in English, we see here the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Now they had to travel a certain distance, did they not, Colonel, to get to this area of responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what is the command post that's applicable to this group which sent its soldiers all the way from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That is the question? All right. Let's take it like this. The 1st Bratunac brigade also left, or some of its forces left its own zone or their own zone or his own zone, and if you look at this, you see that the 1st Bratunac Brigade determines a unit that is to join the Milic Brigade. This is the gist. It carries out a task that was originally given to the Milic Brigade. It has now joined the Milic Brigade, and if you look at subitem or subparagraph 1 you see that it's got its own -- it reports to the commander of the Milic brigade and then it brings it there, a part of the Bratunac Brigade. And there is no need to establish a command post for the Bratunac Brigade. Rather, it carries out the tasks and uses the command post already established by the Milic Brigade in order to have communications with its own command, its own superior command. That is why nothing is determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where is Bracan?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. One should look it up on a map, but if we go to subparagraph 1 it's probably something to do with the Milic Brigade. They mention Bracan as an area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now. We've gone through this whole exercise, but in fact I don't think there is any disagreement that I think you've said twice now that you were in reserve in the village of Podzeplje, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. There is no dispute there. If we could go back to P104. We would just like to tender P1225, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as P1225.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how long were you actually based at Podzeplje?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean the unit as a whole or just the forward command post of the Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just you and your unit, sir, your forces.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The units came after part of the Zvornik Brigade left the area. My unit was given the following task, based on the original decision: I was to follow it within the combat disposition and I was supposed to be introduced as needed. Since he left, I think my unit was introduced on the 16th, pursuant to an order following the departure of the Zvornik Brigade. As far as the forward command post, it remained in Podzeplje until the day it was moved, transferred to the Godjenje sector. And then there was another relocation on or about the 27th, to the Borike sector in reserves. The command element, until the transfer or relocation, stayed until it moved to Godjenje. As far as the combat element, following the departure of the Zvornik Brigade, it was moved to a part of the ground occupied by the forces of the Zvornik Brigade on what I believe was the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And briefly, Colonel, could you tell the Trial Chamber what the reason for the Zvornik Brigade's departure from the Zepa operation was.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: At the briefing, then, which appears to be the popular term these days, while we were reporting to the commander, I think it was the 16th, the 7th, the command post of the corps in Solila, it was said that the Zvornik Brigade had to leave because of certain problems that had occurred in the defence zone of the Zvornik Brigade. There had been a breakthrough at the front end, resulting in casualties on both sides, weapons being seized and so on and so forth, the regional command of the Zvornik Brigade ws sent back with some of his men. I think it was the 16th. Those were the reasons. The forces of the 28th Division that were moving towards Kladanj or whatever area that was in order to link up with the BH Army, on a massive scale, broke through the lines using the weapons they had. The estimates at the time said 2.000 men got through the front end of the Zvornik Brigade and then the forces from Zepa returned to give them a hand and to also take over command in order to deal with the problem which was becoming an obvious problem in the defence zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So clearly, Commander Pandurevic had been in communication with his home brigade based in Zvornik such that he was apprised of these developments and then made the decision to return to his own area of responsibility; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't quite put it in such simple terms. The brigade commander cannot simply leave this area just because he found out and he took the decision. He got an order to go back, to leave this area because he couldn't take the decision himself, whether he would stay there for this long or that long and how long he would spend on a certain mission regardless of any problems that his subordinates in his command post were telling him about. But it's also about what you said in the first part of your question: Yes, the brigade commander did have a link to his command but not a direct link to his command. Whoever informed him about the problems, this was the command post of the corps in Vlasenica which had received their report on what was going on in the defence area of the Zvornik Brigade and then they in turn informed the forward command post, the communication centre there. And then General Krstic, who was in command of the operation overall, took the decision to pull them out and ordered Pandurevic to go back and deal with the situation. That is the essence. It's not like he had a direct link and then the other man told him I'm facing some problems here, come over and give me a hand. It's not quite like that, if you see what I mean. No commander would have been able to make decisions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Of course not, Colonel. And what I want to focus on is what you just focused on, which is the communications link at the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica. I take it that's the same link that you testified you were able to avail yourself of when you were operating in the Srebrenica area. For example, when you were in Bojna and you needed to contact another unit, perhaps your home brigade in Mezina [phoen], you would have had to contact your brigade through that Drina Corps command link or switchboard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The communication lines were functioning as envisaged based on a plan drawn up especially for that mission. Other units were organising combat equipment, men, logistics, and our own logistics officers or communications officers were drawing up a plan for that area for that particular mission, and then, among other things, we had the code name, and that's why, for example, this task was code named Krivaja 95, and it was under that name that everyone knew about it and then there was some manipulation going on. The signals plan, the communications plan that we received from the communications chief, in this case the corps commander, and this was sent to each of the brigades, it detailed the frequencies that we would be using, the fall-back frequencies, what to do when there were problems, what the stand-by systems were to be used, and also the substance of our encrypted communications. We had these codes, we had the call signs, so, for example, the village was Krivaca but we would call it Razvalina. It's just something that we agreed on. Or a different name perhaps, whatever they came up with. And certain features, for example. You could have a certain features marked in the same way for each of the units on the map and then everybody would know that it's Zlovrh number 31, for example. But this is something that each of us needed to get from our signals officer, as well as a communications plan. Therefore, the communications plan was used for the Srebrenica operation. I think it was also used for Stupcanica operation because there were no changes that were introduced because not all of the same units were involved and maybe no changes were made. It might have been reservists I think from the 65th regiment or something like that, maybe that was introduced as a reserve participant, and saw the frequencies and they operated like that in much the same way, but the plan had to be there, there had to be a plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, may I interrupt you. You are speaking very fast. And it's a big problem for the interpreters and the Court Recorder to catch everything what you are saying. Please slow down while giving an answer. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do by best, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel I just note page 56, line 10, the transcript didn't catch the second operation's name. You said, "Therefore the communications plan was used for the Srebrenica operation. I think it was also used for --" and then we have a gap. I think you said the name of the second operation, the Zepa operation. If you could just put that on the record so we have it clear, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally didn't use it at the time but I read the order today, the order for attack. I think the name was Stupcanica. It is possible that the same communications plan was used in the Zepa operation, but I don't know, but I think the name here was Stupcanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just while we are on this topic, and this will be my last question on this subject, I think. You -- and I'll paraphrase you a little bit, but you testified in the Blagojevic case - and this is transcript page 7479, if anybody wants to check - you testified that if you couldn't maintain communications, you couldn't command operations. Can you give the Trial Chamber, please, a little bit of an idea of how important maintaining communications is to an operation or, indeed, the proper functioning of an army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please repeat the reference to the transcript in the Blagojevic case. It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's transcript page 7479, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, please, your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still adhere by that statement. If the communication system had not functioned, when it comes to such complex operations within any system that exists, it can be in finances, in judiciary, and especially in such situations and in such events, it would not have been possible to engage in combat because the command that organised those activities was duty-bound to also coordinate, to listen to reports, to react to the events, in order to prevent unnecessary losses and problems that might have arised if we didn't know where people were, how far people had reached, and there were all sorts of weapons, shells and explosives, that could have been perilous for the troops. Even if we had not planned to go somewhere, if we lost contact with the units and elements that provided logistic support, the entire operation would have to come to a halt on those lines and in such conditions, until such moment when the system was operational again. When we were being prepared for work in military schools, in peacetime and in complex activities, this communication system is the central nervous system of any army, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a new topic, Colonel. In the Popovic trial, you may recall you were shown a very large map that had been signed by General Krstic, it had a cross drawn over the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and four Cyrillic Ss and some statements by General Krstic on the map. Do you recall that from the last trial?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have refreshed my memory. I think -- not only do I think but I'm sure that you have refreshed my memory. I remember having seen that again. But I can't really remember what was written on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we could quickly have 1499 -- I beg your pardon, that's the old number. It's the 2007 number. If we could have P106, please. We don't have the translated version at the moment to show while we're looking at it blown up, but can you just again read what is written to the right of first the Srebrenica enclave here?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: "Srebrenica was Serbian and is Serbian again, on the 12th of July 1995, General Major Krstic."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And below that, next to the Zepa enclave portion of the map, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: "Zepa also is Serbian, on the 27th of July 1995," again General Major Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you looked at this map in the Popovic trial you testified that the movements, the military movements indicated on this map didn't correspond with your recollection of the actual movements on the ground during the operation. But you testified that you do believe that you saw a Krivaja 95 map with General Mladic's signature on it. Is -- have I summarised your prior testimony fairly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case. Maybe I could be shown the map. In any case, this is not a combat document. This map does not represent an official combat document. It is not a map on which decisions were based. This is possibly a working map that was established after the events, and the ones where I saw all those signatures, I believe that that was the decision for Krivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I've got a little surprise for you, but before we leave this exhibit, again we can see that General Krstic has, on both of these enclaves, drawn a cross with these four Ss. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what significance that has for you, if any, and if you have any idea of what significance those symbols had for General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Is that the surprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. There is more.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: What that meant to him, I don't know. But I know that this symbol has been taken from the Serbian flag or the coat of arms of the Republic of Serbia. The four Ss represent the Serbs; the cross and the four Ss symbolise the Serbs. And the coat of arms is now used in Serbia, and those Ss reflect the significance. The graphical symbolism also is reflected in what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your understanding, do those four Ss stand for any words in particular? Are they abbreviations for anything, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This is not how I interpret this symbol. I personally don't have an interpretation. There are all sorts of theoreticians or quasi-theoreticians, when all the notorious things started happening, they provided all sorts of interpretations. I'm not an expert, but in any case I have not interpreted the four Ss in any way. There is no symbolism in the cross. And this is what Krstic drew, and in graphical terms this is a product which was taken from Serbia, and then the wording to the right of the symbols are reflected in the symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you ever heard the saying or the phrase, "Only unity will save the Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you that there have been all sorts of interpretations. Some proposed your version, and there have also been others that studied the history of Orthodox Church in our area, who have proposed other interpretations. I will repeat: I have heard what you have just mentioned but I don't think that even Krstic was among those who would have drawn the symbol because of the meaning. The symbol itself signifies something that belongs to the Serbs, and in this case the sector here depicted in this way is what it is and the interpretation I could provide is that there was no longer any need for any lines because everything belonged to the Serbs. There may be other interpretations of that, but I don't see a context in which the words, "Only unity will save the Serbs" would be necessary given the fact that both ethnic groups died in the area. And now everything is over, the battle is over, and the description is given, this is now Serbian territory, there are no more combat positions or lines in the area. That's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's also fair to say, sir, is it not, that there were no more Muslims in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa at that time.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps. You have suggested you have a surprise for me. I don't want any such surprises but I would not put forth any positions or opinions on that. I'm not going to speculate that somebody on that -- on their side drew their own map and put words on it, "We are no longer there." Let's not speculate with symbolism and things like that. Let's stop right there. This is just an explosion of satisfaction that one segment is over. So if there were five of us here, each of us would be able to propose their own interpretation, and I don't think that it is a good subject for discussion here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just follow up on one thing you said, Colonel. When I asked you that it's also fair to say that there were no more Muslims in the area of Srebrenica and Zepa at that time, your answer was "Perhaps." Is there a question in your mind about whether there were Muslims left in Srebrenica enclave and Zepa enclave after these two operations?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: What you have you just asked me today, is that what you're referring to? Just a minute ago, in the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed, I can repeat it again, if you want, but I think it's a pretty simple question.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we started talking about the map that had already been admitted previously. Well, I don't think that any of them were left there. There is no need to conclude anything differently. After the two operations and the evacuation of people from the area, save for those who had scattered across the area, at the time when I was hospitalised, I must say that there were still soldiers being killed in the zone of defence of my brigade, from those people who hurried through the woods trying to find a way to link up with their own forces, so I would not rule out the fact that there were still Muslims in the area. Well, it's possible that there were still Muslims there because not all of them came out the road, there were still people roaming around trying to link up with their forces. During that time on those days it is possible that there were still Muslims moving about. You may have not understood me when I told you that we shouldn't go along that way. On the 29th, when I was hospitalised, people came to visit and every time they would tell me a few more soldiers were killed in the area where the zone of responsibility of my brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during that period of time that you're speaking of, Colonel, you're referring to what I think is commonly known as a mopping up operation or a search operation, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In any case, none of the two operations ended with the full evacuation of the population, or the entrance into the enclave which were not only narrowed down but even stopped functioning. The scouring of the terrain is a normal activity that follows any combat activity when the area is placed under the control of the unit that was engaged in active combat. It is a rule. It is not only normal but it is a rule to look at the area, to inspect the area, to inspect the roads that could be used by the remains of the enemy elements from which they could open fire on us once we were relaxed; they could kill our command or launch some sabotage activities. This is a normal activity undertaken by every military in the world when territory is placed under control. This is a logical sequence of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think as you said before, the scattered elements of whatever Muslims were left were trying to get out of the enclaves, were they not? They were trying, as you said, to reach free territory.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case, those who did not want to surrender looked for possibilities to reach what they considered free territory. To be very precise: A territory under the control of the Republika Srpska was also free but they did not want to surrender to the Republika Srpska army, they wanted to link up with their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are beyond the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we have to adjourn for the second break. I would like to invite you, Mr. Thayer, to consider the length of the examination-in-chief. We got an estimation that you will need one hour. You are beyond that time already and you should consider the remaining examination-in-chief carefully, taking into account that most of the evidence of the witness is already in evidence. We adjourn and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Please continue and take the -- please be aware of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I promised you a surprise, and we can look at it on e-court but also in full size. About 18 months ago, the OTP interviewed General Zivanovic, and he provided us with a map that we are about to see on e-court, but I want to show you the full-size version because it's much easier for you to see and to assess. And the number is 5519, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we have some problems with e-court, and with the transcript. Perhaps somebody can assist Judge Nyambe and Judge Mindua. Now I'm back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, is that close enough or can you read it well enough from where you are?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead. We have resolved the problems on the screens. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, as I said, we received this map from General Zivanovic about 18 months ago. We did not have it in our possession when you testified in the Popovic case. Does it look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see that it has General Mladic's signature in the upper right-hand -- upper left-hand corner, with the code name Krivaja-95 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, may I interrupt you for a moment? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we please get the same thing in e-court? I don't have it on either of my screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, it's 65 ter 5519, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could, on e-court, upload the translation version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, we can see that in the upper right-hand corner, the operation code name, Krivaja-95, General Mladic's handwriting, saying, "Completed. This was Serbian and it's now Serbian" with a date of 12 July 1995. General Zivanovic's signature at the lower right-hand corner. Do you see that, sir? With the Drina Corps stamp, lower right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, General Mladic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see a signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We need to scroll down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the upper left-hand corner, General Mladic's signature and approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, my first question for you, sir, is: Do the axes of attack that are depicted on this map more closely reflect the events on the ground, as you experienced them, when compared to the other map that we showed you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one thing: Before I answer this question, may I respond by presenting you with a surprise? This is not a map for the operation that was carried out. This is a map for active actions planned for the Drina Corps units holding the lines facing the Srebrenica enclave. You see that the 2nd Romanija Brigade is not shown on this map. I believe "military secret, strictly confidential, Krivaja-95" was added later on. You can tell if you look closely at the marks of the pen that was used. And then in the right corner, something was added also. There is a pointer that I can use, could I please have one? It reads, "forces for active actions or operations" and in the 1st Infantry Battalion of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, that's what it says but I don't see it up there, the 1st Infantry Battalion of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, I don't see it marked anywhere around Srebrenica, just in the additional text further down on the map. And then the infantry battalion from the 1st Vlasenica Brigade, 2nd Romanija Brigade, 2nd Company or MUP station, and so on and so forth. I think these are later additions, not contemporaneous. Because if you look at the deployment of forces around the Srebrenica enclave you can see where my unit was introduced but it doesn't say the 2nd Romanija Brigade. It says the Independent Infantry Battalion Skelani, the 1st Light Infantry Brigade to the right, and the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade to the left. I think the whole thing was added later on, as part of the decision for Krivaja operation. If I may continue, if you have a map that reflects a decision for a certain action at a certain time, you have to see the period in time which that refers to. Active operations decision, for example, the 6th of July, 1995, and that constitutes a combat document for that particular activity. I'll say it again: I think it was General Zivanovic who did this because this map was probably somewhere or other in his office just lying around and then the map was designed based on directive number 7 in which the Drina Corps was told to be carrying out active operations over the following year, and this is a fair reflection of that but it is not a fair reflection of the actual operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we see on the map on the screen a different version than that which is originally put to the witness. This is a problem because here are these entries in English which obviously are translations. But it would be more helpful for the Chamber to have the original version on the screen, and when I ask, I can't see a signature by Mr. Zivanovic. You didn't dwell on that. I would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll point it out, Mr. President. If we could have the original version, please. And it may be useful as well to hand up the full-size to the Trial Chamber so you can see it better. The problem with this version in the original on e-court, Mr. President, is it's not quite as good a copy as the one with the translations, but we can try to blow up that bottom right-hand corner and see if we can catch the signature. As you can see, this map is a little darker than the previous one. The signature, if you see the stamp, Mr. President, and I think Colonel Trivic can weigh in if he can see it as well on the original but there is a -- you can see some squiggly lines in a bluish colour ink that flow from left to right starting with basically with that circular stamp there. Again, it's harder to see on this version but we can hand up the full-size original for the Trial Chamber to take a look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear from the witness if he sees the original signature of a person on the right bottom corner. On the original map. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is enough. But, Mr. Thayer, again, can you give us an indication of the length of the remaining examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have one more exhibit, which is the diary of Colonel Trivic, to review some entries with him, and that's it. I'll probably need to the end of the session to complete those questions with Colonel Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's only a question of fairness. Several times I asked Mr. Tolimir to give an indication of the length of his examination, and therefore I asked you the same line. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us, Colonel, what the map that you remember seeing looked like and how it differed from this one?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember what that map looked like but I'm looking at what this map indicates and, based on what is there as well as in the rules for drawing up this type of map for this task in July, all of the units involved in active operations were supposed to be displayed on the map, based on the order for readiness on the 6th of July 1995. If we wanted to pursue this all the way, and link the whole thing up, it would be necessary to look at the substance of what the order says and then trace every single element of the combat disposition and all of the units mentioned in that document as having a task in July, in terms of active operations. All of these units would have to be graphically represented or depicted on this map, as well as its axes. My unit is not there, which is a clear indicator, to my mind, that this map was produced in order to carry out the task from the directive of a course of active operations being planned but not active operations of this type to narrow down or extend the enclave. Rather, actions involving the forces that were holding the positions facing the enclave, and that's why my unit is not there. Secondly, my observation suggests that there is no depiction here of the elements of the Zvornik Brigade. Have a look for yourself. You can check in the English version too. And some other units, too, that are not there. These are merely the units that were holding those positions facing the Srebrenica enclave. Hence, my inference that this map is not a faithful reflection of the order. What the text of the order says must be graphically depicted on a map. You can talk to one of your experts and I have no doubt that they will confirm what I'm telling you. And you can analyse this all over again. Yes, Mladic's signature is there, but some bits of the text were added later on, and then they added the 2nd Romanija Brigade. I think if you consult a handwriting expert, they can confirm that. Maybe this was done by several different people at different points in time. If you look at the mark that the pen leaves here, where it says, "I hereby approve," and in the lower right corner it is not the same pen being used, it's not the same ink. This is fresh ink and this is old ink, an old pen being used, as far as I can tell. Therefore, this map suffered later editions, in a manner of speaking, in order to have a map that would be a map of this operation, and I can't rule this out. Mladic's signature is there, Zivanovic, and undertaking good relations to the chief of the Main Staff, he probably just showed him this map and, you know, it was just like that; they simply decided to take advantage of the moment, here, let me sign this as well, because he hadn't signed it up until that point in time, and he also put his signature right here where it says "completed." You know, it was just a situation in an office somewhere. Maybe he simply dropped by and met up with Tomo Kovac, maybe it was something like that, in the corps commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I can just summarise one portion of that answer, sir. The map itself, your testimony is that it reflects the intentions of the superior command at a particular point in time. What you're saying is just not during the actual operations that were conducted in July of 1995. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the basic conclusion, yes. You know the substance of this. I listened to it, we talked about the substance of Directive 7 and 7.1 for that year in 1995 in which the Drina Corps -- and I'm talking about during my proofing, when I was listening to all these materials, that Drina Corps faced the following task -- rather, it was set out for them how they should be carrying out their tasks in the next year. The Supreme Command issued a directive and the Main Staff distributed that to all of the subordinate units. That task, that directive, gives out tasks to all of the units, and the Drina Corps had the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in its own area of responsibility, and then the Drina Corps received the task of carrying out active combat operations, improving their positions, cutting across the enemy's communication lines between Srebrenica and Zepa, as enclaves and so on and so forth, and it was based on that directive that steps were taken in order to be able to say there you go -- you see Zepa -- why is Zepa not there? Was it later on? But then you have the arrows pointing this way and that way meaning there were operations being carried out there as well of one sort or another. Therefore this map probably reflects a directive, probably an order that the corps commander or the corps command added to this map or wrote in addition to this map. When you have active combat operations being carried out, they have to indicate clearly. Where is the Zvornik Brigade Battalion, where is the Romanija Brigade? I'm not saying it was along one of the main roads but it was, you know, somewhere close to the focus of these active operations. All I'm saying is it simply wasn't shown anywhere on this map and that leads me to believe that this map does not reflect the order for July; in other words, Krivaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, may I remind you to slow down while speaking. It was extremely fast. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 5519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't want the Trial Chamber to feel left out, so we have a surprise for the Trial Chamber as well today. We have some hard copies of this diary that the Trial Chamber has heard references to. I don't need to belabour the origin of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you bring your diary with you into court today? Do you have it in your briefcase?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The maps [sic] will be received in the original or original copy, and the Defence -- I see Mr. Gajic has already a copy of that. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may hand up a copy to the witness as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, if you would take out your copy, the original of the notebook, and just place it next to this reproduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was erring when I said the maps should be given to the Chamber. It was the copy of the diary. I was not aware of that. I just want to put it on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if you would kindly allow the Trial Chamber, if it wishes, just to see what this notebook looks like up close, we can hand it up just for a moment to the Trial Chamber. It's a very delicate document; you'll see that the glue has become undone and the pages are loose. Colonel, will you permit the court assistant just to hand that up to the Trial Chamber to get a sense of what it is? Thank you. Will you agree that it's a fairly standard notebook that you cut down to size to use during these events?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your testimony in the Blagojevic case, did you place some pages that had come out back in the proper chronological order and then number the pages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After having used the diary, not only in the courtroom but during the proofing session, the notebook just came loose and the chronological order was lost. In order to prevent that from happening again, I marked all the pages with a red felt-tipped pen. I hope I had put all the pages in order. You will see that some of the pages are the summaries of what had happened over the past couple of days, and then you will see that I have written on both sides of the pages and that all the sides on one side contain information about Srebrenica, and the other, the verso, contains information about Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So basically you wrote on both sides of the pages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when it came to the Zepa operation, what did you do in terms of starting that section of this diary?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This is what I just said. I turned the notebook upside down and started writing from the back of the same notebook, and went forward into the notebook. So Srebrenica starts on the right side of the notebook, and Zepa starts on the back side of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have had the opportunity to have a very brief look at it, and the notebook was -- the diary was given back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look on e-court, and this is 65 ter 7108. I just want to take us through, as we go through our copies of the hard copy, so we can explain how this has been reproduced. We see in e-court here ERN number 0648-6772, and is it fair to say, sir, that what this image is of is the cover, the hard cardboard cover, of your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the next page in e-court, and if we just open the hard copy to the next page, which is 0648-6773, is what we have displayed here the flip side or the opposite side of that cardboard cover page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page -- actually, let's just stay on here for one quick sec. I note here there is a date of 15 July 1995 and that you've written this on the back of the cover. Is that in chronological order or does that reference something you wrote down at a different time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This is not in a chronological order. This was noted on the 15th of July, in the course of our preparations for active combat around Zepa. These are channels and code numbers for the links to those who were my immediate contacts. I used the flip side of the cover page to note that all the way down to the 0, if you can see that, something that looks like a bull's eye. This is my note of the frequencies that were used; 147275, Veljko was 101; Srna, which was a code unit -- code name of a unit, had different code; and finally Vuk Kosoric had his own channels and I could communicate with him by radio on the channels indicated here. You see Dr. Mira Djeric. Everything up to there was noted on the 15th of July. The second part, the bottom part, starting with Dr. Mira Djeric and the telephone numbers, if you allow me to explain the page to you, Dr. Mira Djeric was a doctor who worked in the military hospital where I was hospitalised after having been wounded. Her husband, Miso, and you can see his number here, he's also a doctor, a neuropsychiatrist, in the same hospital. I noted their home number and also the telephone number of Dr. Stojanovic, who admitted me when I was first brought to the hospital, as well as the director of the hospital, Dr. Tausan's number. But that bottom part -- half of the page was filled while I was in the hospital, which means that the bottom half of the page does not concern the time when Srebrenica operation was underway because that was not noted on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you've just used this inside cover page as some free space to jot down certain things as you needed them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we go to the next page, which is 0648-6774, we see here a date of 5 July 1995, and the number 1 in red ink. Can you tell us what is going on on this page and what that red numbering is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: On this page, you can see that this page was filled in the Zeleni Jadar sector, which is where the unit arrived from the Defence sector, and that shows the strength of my unit. And of those who were also deployed there, you can see Sekovici, 140. That is the numerical strength of my unit, and all of the other units of the brigade. And number 1 in red was entered once the pages came loose. I put them back together and then I marked them in red in order to have the pages in the right chronological order, to reflect the flow of events that are described in the notebook, the events that took place during the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just go to the next page, which is 0648-6775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is a technical problem again. Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can work with the hard copies in the meantime, Mr. President, we all have them in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we look at 0648-6775, I take it that that is the flip side or the other side of the page we just looked at which you had marked with the number 1 at the top; is that fair to say? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the flip side of the first page, to put it that way: The following page depicts number 2. It may have been an error on my part. I marked the pages but only on its front side, not on its flip side. And that's how it goes in the notebook all the way to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly what needed to be explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we are now, Mr. President, at the end of the day. Mr. President, I did have some substantive questions for the diary. It's taken a little longer to explain it. So I will, with the Court's indulgence, have some more substantive questions on specific items that were not raised in the prior trial but which shouldn't take too much longer now that we've kind of got the rhythm. I can just take us to the pages in the hard copy on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, this concerns the Chamber because you indicated some days ago that you will need one hour, I think now you have used two and a half or something like that. I have no exact information. You always should consider to dwell on those parts of the testimony which was not part of the previous case. Are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do intend to tender it, Mr. President. I can do that now. And again, that's 65 ter 7108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01444. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day. We will resume on Thursday in the morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Sir, you should be reminded it's not allowed to have any contact with the parties during the break. I think I have to repeat the last piece. Please put your ear-phones on. I just said you are not allowed to have any contact with the parties during the break, and we will resume on Thursday at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, 9 December 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
